title: Mutual Aid in Drohiczyn: Care for the Sick, the Poor, and Travelers
summary: Charitable institutions in the records offer a clear view of how residents organized practical support for vulnerable neighbors and visitors.
editorialContent:
![A view of Drohiczyn](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Drohiczyn_Zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_klasztorny_jezuit%C3%B3w_06.jpg/1920px-Drohiczyn_Zesp%C3%B3%C5%82_klasztorny_jezuit%C3%B3w_06.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail)

## A town organised around care

In the [Drohiczyn Jewish community](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_39d23dc1ff780fc5e0705ad8), care was not only a private family matter. The memorial book remembers a network of charitable societies that stepped in when illness, poverty, travel, or death placed demands on people beyond what a household could manage. Its surviving records name the institutions, some of their members and leaders, but offer only brief glimpses of their everyday work.

Two societies appear under overlapping names. [Linat ha-Tzedek](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_f0e4604f0b339e8fb9d90e94) is described as helping poor sick people obtain doctors and medicines; the [Bikur Cholim society](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_5f611337669bc0bc1fcbc202) is given much the same task. A second Bikur Cholim record describes aid to local people in need as well as travelers and guests. These accounts may reflect overlapping responsibilities, changing practice, or distinct branches of work. The records do not settle which explanation is right, so it would be misleading to assign each duty exclusively to one society.

## Medicine, money, and personal attention

The memorial book connects [Gdalya Grossman](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_f0e4604f0b339e8fb9d90e94) with Linat ha-Tzedek as a member, and names [Hershel Chaim Lev](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_f0e4604f0b339e8fb9d90e94) as its leader. Another record identifies Hershl Khayim Lev among four delegates who met the German commandant. The similar names plausibly refer to the same person, but the material provided does not establish that identity. It does show how the memorial book’s institutional and wartime records can intersect without fully explaining their connection.

The name *Bikur Cholim* means visiting the sick, and the societies’ recorded remit was practical as well as compassionate: access to medical help and medicines for people who could not readily afford them. The book does not specify how doctors were selected, how medicines were paid for, or how much assistance any one family received. Nor does it give a date for the societies’ founding. Those gaps matter: the evidence preserves the purpose of the work more clearly than its administrative details.

## Hospitality and the wider charitable world

The second Bikur Cholim account extends mutual aid beyond illness, naming local needy people, travelers, and guests. That breadth fits a town in which people might arrive without kin or secure lodging. But the supplied Drohiczyn record does not say whether the society maintained a hostel, arranged meals in private homes, or provided cash; it establishes the obligation of hospitality, not its exact arrangements. The book’s contents separately list a chapter titled “A Letter about the Medical Assistance Organization and Traveler’s Hostel,” a promising lead for understanding how these responsibilities were organised.

Comparable memorial-book testimony from other towns helps show what such charitable language could mean in practice—but it is not evidence that Drohiczyn followed the same exact customs. In Derechin, a memoir describes Bikur Cholim arranging doctors or medical practitioners and medicines, while Linat Tzedek volunteers kept night watch at the bedside and relieved relatives. It also recalls regular collections and food preparations for sick people. This comparison suggests the range of service that similar institutions could provide, while leaving Drohiczyn’s precise routines unresolved. ([jewishgen.org](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Derechin1/der150.html?utm_source=openai))

## Care at death—and the limits of the record

The [Chevra Kadisha](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_c5d7a2d1a7279ebd5ce8b27c), or burial society, appears among the town’s religious and cultural institutions. [Dov Varshavski](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_c5d7a2d1a7279ebd5ce8b27c) is named as a member, and [Moses Aaron Berg](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_c5d7a2d1a7279ebd5ce8b27c) as its leader. The record signals an organised communal responsibility at death, but does not describe its procedures or establish whether the society also supported bereaved families. Those details should not be supplied from general custom and mistaken for Drohiczyn testimony.

The memorial book also recalls [Moshe Freger](/communities/drohiczyn/records/mention_9758b223085348208a7d3b78), a *shochet* who sometimes helped his grandfather distribute charity. That small detail widens the picture: relief could depend not only on formal societies but also on trusted people carrying aid into households. The record does not name the grandfather or say who received the distributions, leaving both as worthwhile questions for further research.

The wider historical record gives the charitable work a stark chronology. Yad Vashem’s *Encyclopedia of the Ghettos* describes Drohiczyn as a town in prewar Poland, with about 800 Jews before the war—roughly two-thirds of its population. It records German occupation on June 22, 1941, the creation of a ghetto in April 1942, and the deportation of those remaining after the November 2, 1942 roundup to Siemiatycze and then to Treblinka. That account does not discuss Linat ha-Tzedek or Bikur Cholim specifically; it provides the wartime context, not independent confirmation of the societies’ work. ([wwv.yadvashem.org](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=258))

Mutual aid in Drohiczyn emerges, then, not as a single institution’s story but as a shared civic practice: medical help, relief for the needy, welcome for strangers, and communal responsibility at death. The memorial book preserves names and purposes, while leaving many daily details beyond recovery. Its fragments are valuable precisely because they show care as organised work—and because they remind us that a community’s surviving account can never contain every household, recipient, or act of kindness.
